en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Aśvajit, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Listen all to what I say."

It is difficult to bring about this end: parents give birth to a child and nourish them with breast milk; as the child grows, they wish to have them behold the light of the sun and moon; the parents display all the myriad things of the world to their child, desiring to cause them to know good and evil.
"O Bhikṣus!

Suppose a son were to carry his father on one shoulder and his mother on the other, continuing until the end of his life; and suppose he were further to adorn their bodies with celestial treasures, moon-bright pearls, jade discs, lapis lazuli, coral, and naturally occurring pearls from birds and beasts—yet even so, he would still not have fully repaid the debt of gratitude owed to his parents."
If one's parents take pleasure in killing living beings, the child should be able to admonish and stop them, ensuring they no longer kill;
if the parents harbor evil intentions, the child should constantly admonish and stop them, ensuring they always mindfully contemplate what is wholesome and remain free from evil intent;
and if the parents are ignorant and lacking wisdom, not knowing the Way of the scriptures, the child should inform them by means of the Buddha’s sutras.
If parents are greedy, fierce, and jealous, the child should follow them and offer gentle admonition;
if parents do not distinguish between good and evil, the child should gradually inform them with gentleness. O Bhikṣus!
My son, you should be like this:

as a child serving your parents, if you desire your clothing to be finer than your parents', your food to be sweeter than your parents', and your speech to be loftier than your parents', then after death you shall enter hell.
"When one becomes a son, he ought to serve his parents with filial piety; those who maintain such conduct shall, upon death, be reborn in the heavens.
All the bhikṣus bowed their heads in reverence and together received this excellent teaching.
The Buddha said:
"There was a great and virtuous upāsaka named Śuddhoda. He took a wife for his son; her name was Yashodharā.
Yashodharā was the daughter of a very wealthy family, yet for many years she did not serve her mother-in-law with the proper etiquette, nor did she respect her husband."
Sudatta was also a virtuous upāsaka; remaining silent and speechless, he went to where the Buddha was and reproached himself, saying:
"I took a wife for my son from the family of a wealthy nobleman of the kingdom, and my heart was filled with great joy."
"She has served me for several years now, yet she is arrogant and self-indulgent, failing to observe the proprieties of a wife; I pray that the Buddha will deign to visit my home tomorrow.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond. By remaining silent, he signaled his intention to go there the following morning.

The next day, when the Buddha arrived at the house of Sudatta, his wife did not come out. The Buddha transformed her through his supernormal powers; her heart was filled with joy, and she finally came out to see the Buddha, whereupon she stepped forward and paid him homage.
The Buddha asked,
"When you were a wife to a man, what did you do for your husband? Yuyé replied:
"One should serve one's husband with the body.
The Buddha said:
"In the way a wife serves her husband, there are three evils and four virtues."
What are the three evils?
The first evil is as follows: dwelling with a lazy person who has no desire to work, who scolds until evening, and who is fond of fine things and quarreling.

The second evil is as follows: it is like living with an enemy; she does not maintain a single-minded devotion toward her husband, she does not wish for his well-being, she does not wish for his success, but rather wishes for his death.

The three evils are as follows: living together with a thief, not cherishing one's husband's property but constantly thinking only of deceiving him; always desiring to beautify oneself while being disobedient to one's children and grandchildren, and thinking only of lewdness and dissipation.
One who dies in such a manner will transmigrate through the evil realms with no time of escape; this is the third evil.
What are the four virtues?

The first virtue is that when a wife sees her husband returning from outside, she should regard him as a mother regards her son; whether he faces urgency or distress, she always desires to take his place with her own body.

Regarding the second type of virtuous woman: she serves her husband as a younger brother serves his elder brother, with the superior and subordinate supporting and serving one another. She does not regard her husband’s faults as faults; she harbors no thoughts of lewdness or dissipation, but always follows her husband’s words.

Regarding the three virtues: a wife should serve her husband as she would a friend; whenever they meet, they should think of one another. When the husband returns from abroad, she should regard him as she would her father or elder brother, welcoming him with a joyful heart and a serene countenance; this is how a wife should maintain her mind.

Regarding the four virtues: a wife should serve her husband as a maidservant; even if he scolds her severely, she should not consider it evil; even if he strikes her, she should not consider it grievous; even if he sends her on errands, she should not consider it laborious. Though the husband may be wicked, she should always think of serving him well and remain mindful of their children and grandchildren. One who dies in such a manner will always be reborn in the heavens, where there will be many attendants, and fine garments and precious jewels will always be upon her person.
The Buddha said, "There are three evil paths and four virtuous ones; which among these do you wish to follow in serving your husband?
Yuye replied:

"A wife serving her husband must not employ three evils; one may dwell together with those who possess four virtues. From this day forward, I pray to serve you as a maidservant serves the son of a great house."
"Yuye immediately crawled on her knees to serve Asudata, attending to her husband according to the rites due between a wife and her spouse."—
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Asudata.
